confidence_note: The 1,600-student finding and 0.7 correlation are Achor's own first-person claim, quoted by Farnam Street and a chapter abstract; Vaillant's 'love' summary and the 'Very Happy People' finding are also in the chapter. The old text's 'two groups at the same stress level', oxytocin/cortisol claims and the weekly-message advice are not supported and dropped. Correlational study: no causal claim beyond Achor's interpretation.
facts: At Harvard, Achor watched students under heavy pressure turn inward, away from friends and family, just when they needed support most.

Achor notes that after arriving at Harvard students face a harsh realization: half of them are now below average; used to being the best, they fall hard, and the depression that follows pulls them inward.

His study of about 1,600 Harvard undergraduates found social support a far greater predictor of happiness than any other factor measured, more than GPA, family income, SAT scores, age, gender or race.
The correlation between social support and happiness was 0.7; Achor notes most psychology findings count as significant around 0.3.
In the 'Very Happy People' study, the one trait that set the happiest 10% apart was the strength of their social relationships.
The Harvard Men Study followed 268 men from college entry in the late 1930s; in 2009 its long-time director George Vaillant summed up the findings in one word: love.
Achor: the most successful people hold tighter to their social support under stress; instead of divesting, they invest.
Vaillant added: seventy years of evidence that our relationships with other people matter, and matter more than anything else in the world.
scene_details: a student alone with the books during exam pressure
tension: Under stress, the smart move feels like pulling away to work harder, and Achor's data point the other way.
opening_idea: Open on Harvard students in exam season shutting the door and dropping friends to study more.

lessons.idea: When pressure rises, keep one standing contact instead of cancelling it.
lessons.anchor: social support predicted happiness more than GPA or income

reflect_final: During your last stressful stretch, which person did you drop first, and what would a ten-minute call with them look like this week?

use_cases.situation: A colleague is skipping lunches to catch up
use_cases.move: Mention that in Achor's 1,600-student study, support beat grades and income; invite them for a short lunch.

use_cases.situation: You are about to cancel plans because of a deadline
use_cases.move: Shorten the plan instead of cancelling it.

use_cases.situation: A friend goes quiet during a hard time
use_cases.move: Send a short message without asking for a reply.

pocket_idea: Under pressure, Harvard's happiest students held on to people; keep one meeting you'd want to cancel.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: In a study of 1,600 Harvard students, friends predicted happiness better than grades, income or SAT scores.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Stressed students turning inward; Achor's 1,600 study; 0.7; Vaillant's 'love'; invest, don't divest.
